name: statistics
title: Statistics
scope: Introductory statistics for center and spread, and for reading a histogram, a normal distribution, or a null hypothesis without overclaiming.
method: Define the question in measurable terms.
Name the units of every variable.
Say whether the numbers are a sample or the whole population.
Choose the statistic that answers the question.
Compute it with the sample formula or the population formula, not a mix.
State the caveat: a histogram, a normal curve, or a null hypothesis does not by itself prove the claim.

formulas.name: Sample mean
formulas.use: The arithmetic average of the n observed sample values.

formulas.name: Sample median
formulas.expr: middle ordered value; if n is even, average the two middle values
formulas.use: A center that extreme values pull less than they pull the mean.

formulas.name: Sample variance
formulas.use: Sample variance divides by n-1, the usual sample estimate of population spread.

formulas.name: Population variance
formulas.use: Population variance divides by N, the population size, not by n-1.

formulas.name: Sample standard deviation
formulas.use: The square root of the sample variance, back in the original units.

formulas.name: z-score
formulas.use: How many population standard deviations x lies from the population mean μ.

formulas.name: Interquartile range
formulas.use: The spread of the middle half; state the quartile rule because textbooks split halves differently.

checks: Sample variance divides by n-1, and population variance divides by N.
Order the values before the median, Q1, Q3, or the interquartile range.
This z-score uses population μ and σ, not the sample mean and s.
Read a histogram as counts in chosen bins, not as proof of a normal distribution.
limits: Swapping the N divisor and the n-1 divisor is incorrect.
A bell-shaped histogram does not prove a normal distribution.
Failing to reject a null hypothesis is not proof that the null hypothesis is true.
